# Education in Pakistan
Education in Pakistan follows a system largely inspired by the English educational model and comprises pre-school (ages 3–5), primary (years 1–5), middle (years 6–8), secondary (years 9–10), intermediate (years 11–12), and tertiary education stages. Primary education includes subjects like Arts, Science, Modern languages, Mathematics, Religious and Social Studies, with provincial languages and foreign languages also taught in some areas. Secondary education culminates in the Secondary School Certificate (SSC), followed by intermediate education leading to the Higher Secondary School Certificate (HSSC). Alternative qualifications such as GCE O/A Levels and vocational education through technical boards are also prevalent. Despite education being free at lower levels, only about 67.5% finish primary school, and public expenditure on education remains low at around 2% of GDP.
Gender disparity is significant, with females underrepresented especially in rural and poorer areas, and cultural and infrastructural barriers affecting female enrollment and retention. Women have begun to progress in higher education but still face systemic challenges. Teacher training suffers from a lack of qualified staff and practical focus, contributing to low educational quality marked by outdated curricula and rote learning methods. Madrassas serve as alternative education for many poor families but are controversial for their conservative teachings. Efforts to improve education include reforms for teacher training, digital and distance learning programs like Teleschool, and government plans to increase education spending. However, structural, social, and quality challenges continue to impede broad educational advancement in Pakistan.
